title: Stability
description: Decide stability from the closed-loop poles and find stable gain ranges with the Routh–Hurwitz test.

study.title: Stability and poles
study.body:
A linear system is (BIBO) **stable** if every bounded input gives a bounded output. For a transfer function this means: all **closed-loop poles in the left half-plane** (negative real parts). Each pole $p$ adds a term $e^{pt}$ to the response.
- All poles with $\text{Re}(p) < 0$: stable, the response decays.
- Any pole with $\text{Re}(p) > 0$: unstable, it grows.
- Simple poles on the $j\omega$ axis (none to the right): **marginally stable**, sustained oscillation.

study.title: Quick checks on the polynomial
study.body:
The closed-loop poles are the roots of the characteristic polynomial $a_ns^n + \dots + a_1s + a_0$ (from $1 + GH = 0$).
- **Necessary:** all coefficients present and of the same sign. A missing term or a sign change means unstable (or at best marginal).
- For order 1 and 2 this is also **sufficient**.
- For order 3, $a_3s^3 + a_2s^2 + a_1s + a_0$ (all positive) is stable if and only if:

study.title: The Routh array
study.body: Write the coefficients in two rows (alternating), then build each new row from the two above it. The number of **sign changes in the first column** equals the number of right-half-plane poles. No sign changes: stable.
study.formula: \begin{array}{c|cc} s^3 & a_3 & a_1 \\ s^2 & a_2 & a_0 \\ s^1 & b_1 & 0 \\ s^0 & a_0 & \end{array} \quad b_1 = \frac{a_2a_1 - a_3a_0}{a_2}

study.title: Fourth order
study.body:
For $s^4 + a_3s^3 + a_2s^2 + a_1s + a_0$ the rows are $[1,\ a_2,\ a_0]$, $[a_3,\ a_1]$, then
- $b_1 = \frac{a_3a_2 - a_1}{a_3}$, $b_2 = a_0$
- $c_1 = \frac{b_1a_1 - a_3a_0}{b_1}$
- last row $a_0$.
Stable if $a_3$, $b_1$, $c_1$, $a_0$ are all positive. Every element of a row can be scaled by a positive number to simplify.

study.title: Range of K and marginal stability
study.body: With a gain $K$ in the loop, the first-column entries depend on $K$; requiring all of them positive gives the stable range. Example: $G = \frac{K}{s(s+1)(s+2)}$ gives $s^3 + 3s^2 + 2s + K$: $b_1 = (6 - K)/3$, so $0 < K < 6$. At $K = 6$ the $s^1$ row is zero: the **auxiliary polynomial** from the $s^2$ row, $3s^2 + 6 = 0$, gives poles at $\pm j\sqrt2$: the loop oscillates at $\omega = \sqrt2$ rad/s.

steps.title: Where are the poles?
steps.body: Each closed-loop pole $p$ contributes a term $e^{pt}$ to the response. If $p$ has a negative real part the term decays; a positive real part makes it grow. So a feedback loop is **stable** when all its closed-loop poles lie in the **left half-plane**.

steps.prompt: Each graph shows the closed-loop poles of a system (σ horizontal, jω vertical, the vertical line is the $j\omega$ axis). Which system is **unstable**?
steps.explanation: Only the first map has poles to the right of the $j\omega$ axis ($0.7 \pm j1.5$): their terms $e^{0.7t}\sin(1.5t)$ grow without bound. Poles close to the axis (like $-0.3$ or $-0.5 \pm j2$) are still stable, just slow to decay.

steps.prompt: A closed loop has poles at $s = -{{a}}$ and $s = {{sg}} \pm j{{w}}$. The loop is stable.
steps.explanation: Stability needs **every** pole in the left half-plane. The real pole $-{{a}}$ is fine. The complex pair has real part {{sg}}, so its terms behave like $e^{ {{sg}}t}$: a negative real part means they decay, a positive one means they grow without bound, and then the whole loop is unstable even though the real pole is fine.

steps.title: The characteristic polynomial
steps.body: The closed-loop poles are the roots of $1 + G(s)H(s) = 0$, written as a polynomial. A quick necessary check: **all coefficients must be present and have the same sign**. If one is missing or negative, the loop is not stable. For first- and second-order polynomials, positive coefficients are also enough.

steps.prompt: Which characteristic polynomial **can** belong to a stable system?
steps.explanation: A negative coefficient ($-2s^2$) or a missing term ($s^2$ in $s^3 + 3s + 2$, $s^2$ in the quartic) rules out stability straight away. $s^3 + 2s^2 + 3s + 1$ passes the quick check and also the third-order test: $a_2a_1 = 6 > a_3a_0 = 1$, so it is stable.

steps.title: The Routh array
steps.body: For higher orders, the coefficient check is not enough. The **Routh array** tells how many poles are in the right half-plane without solving for them: write the coefficients in two rows, compute the next rows, and count the **sign changes in the first column**.
steps.formula: \begin{array}{c|cc} s^3 & a_3 & a_1 \\ s^2 & a_2 & a_0 \\ s^1 & b_1 & 0 \\ s^0 & a_0 & \end{array} \quad b_1 = \frac{a_2a_1 - a_3a_0}{a_2}

steps.prompt: Build the Routh array of $s^3 + {{a2}}s^2 + {{a1}}s + {{a0}}$. What is the first-column entry $b_1$ of the $s^1$ row?
How many closed-loop poles of $s^3 + {{a}}s^2 + {{b}}s + {{c}}$ lie in the right half-plane?
steps.explanation: First column: 1, {{a}}, $b_1 = \frac{{{a}}\cdot{{b}} - {{c}}}{{{a}}}$ = {{(a*b-c)/a}}, {{c}}. Count the sign changes: {{2*step(c-a*b)}}. (Going from positive to negative and back counts twice.)

steps.prompt: A polynomial with all coefficients positive can still have roots in the right half-plane.
steps.explanation: Positive coefficients are necessary but, from third order on, not sufficient. Example: $s^3 + s^2 + s + 6$ has $b_1 = (1 - 6)/1 = -5$: two sign changes, two right-half-plane poles.

steps.prompt: $G(s) = \frac{K}{s(s+{{a}})(s+{{b}})}$ with unity negative feedback. Find the largest $K$ for which the loop is stable.
$G(s) = \frac{K}{s(s+{{a}})(s+{{b}})}$ with unity feedback is set to the critical gain $K = {{a*b*(a+b)}}$. At what frequency does the loop oscillate?
steps.explanation: At the critical gain the $s^1$ row is zero. The $s^2$ row gives the auxiliary polynomial ${{a+b}}s^2 + {{a*b*(a+b)}} = 0$, so $s^2 = -{{a*b}}$ and $s = \pm j\sqrt{{{a*b}}}$: $\omega$ = {{sqrt(a*b)}} rad/s.

steps.prompt: $G(s) = \frac{K}{(s+{{a}})^3}$ with unity feedback. Find the largest $K$ for stability.
$G(s) = \frac{K}{s(s+{{p}})(s+{{2*p}})(s+{{3*p}})}$ with unity feedback gives $s^4 + {{c3}}s^3 + {{c2}}s^2 + {{c1}}s + K = 0$.

ask.prompt: At the critical $K$, find the oscillation frequency.
ask.explanation: Critical $K = \frac{b_1a_1}{a_3}$ = {{10*p^4}}. Auxiliary polynomial from the $s^2$ row: ${{b1}}s^2 + {{10*p^4}} = 0$, so $\omega = \sqrt{{{10*p^4}}/{{b1}}}$ = {{p}} rad/s.

steps.prompt: The first column of a Routh array reads $1,\ 4,\ -2,\ 3,\ 5$. How many poles lie in the right half-plane?
steps.explanation: Follow the signs: $+$ to $+$ (no change), $+$ to $-$ (change), $-$ to $+$ (change), $+$ to $+$ (no change). Two sign changes, so two right-half-plane poles. The value of the negative entry does not matter, only its sign.

steps.prompt: A PI-type controller gives $G(s) = \frac{K(s+{{z}})}{s(s+{{a}})(s+{{b}})}$ with unity feedback. Find the largest $K$ for stability.
steps.explanation: $s^3 + {{a+b}}s^2 + ({{a*b}} + K)s + {{z}}K = 0$. Condition: ${{a+b}}({{a*b}} + K) > {{z}}K$, i.e. ${{(a+b)*a*b}} > ({{z}} - {{a+b}})K$, so $K <$ {{(a+b)*a*b}}/{{d}} = {{(a+b)*a*b/d}}. The zero far to the left ({{-z}}) is what limits the gain.

steps.prompt: A loop has the characteristic equation $s^3 + {{a}}s^2 + (K - {{b}})s + K = 0$. Find the **smallest** $K$ for which it is stable.
steps.explanation: First column: 1, {{a}}, $b_1 = \frac{{{a}}(K - {{b}}) - K}{{{a}}}$, $K$. $b_1 > 0$: ${{a-1}}K > {{a*b}}$, so $K >$ {{a*b/(a-1)}}. This also satisfies $K > {{b}}$ (the $s$ coefficient) and $K > 0$, so the loop is stable for $K >$ {{a*b/(a-1)}}.

steps.prompt: If a whole row of the Routh array becomes zero, the polynomial has roots placed symmetrically about the origin, for example a pair on the $j\omega$ axis.
steps.explanation: A zero row means the polynomial has an even factor (the auxiliary polynomial from the row above), whose roots come in pairs $\pm p$. At a critical gain this is typically $\pm j\omega$: marginal stability and a sustained oscillation at $\omega$.

ask.prompt: Find the critical gain $K$ (edge of stability).
Find the oscillation frequency at the critical gain.
ask.explanation: At $K_{crit}$ = {{c2*c1-c0}}, the auxiliary polynomial is ${{c2}}s^2 + {{c0}} + K = {{c2}}s^2 + {{c2*c1}} = 0$, so $\omega = \sqrt{{{c1}}}$ = {{sqrt(c1)}} rad/s.

steps.prompt: How many roots of $s^4 + 2s^3 + 3s^2 + 4s + 5$ lie in the right half-plane?
steps.explanation: Rows: $[1,\ 3,\ 5]$, $[2,\ 4]$. $b_1 = (2\cdot3 - 4)/2 = 1$, $b_2 = 5$. $c_1 = (1\cdot4 - 2\cdot5)/1 = -6$. Last row: 5. First column $1, 2, 1, -6, 5$: two sign changes, so two right-half-plane roots, even though every coefficient is positive.

steps.prompt: $G(s) = \frac{K}{s(s+{{a}})(s+{{b}})}$ runs with $K$ = {{K}}. By what factor can $K$ be increased before the loop goes unstable? Give it in dB (this is the **gain margin**).
steps.explanation: Critical gain from Routh: $K_{crit} = {{a+b}}\cdot{{a*b}}$ = {{Km}}. Factor: {{Km}}/{{K}} = {{1/f}}, i.e. $20\log_{10}({{1/f}})$ = {{20*log10(1/f)|dB}}.

steps.prompt: A system whose transfer function has one pole at $s = 0$ and all other poles in the left half-plane is BIBO stable.
steps.explanation: It is only **marginally** stable. A pole at the origin is an integrator: a bounded step input produces a ramp output that grows without bound. BIBO stability requires every pole strictly in the left half-plane.

steps.prompt: Put the steps for finding the stable range of $K$ in order.
items: Check that all coefficients can be positive
Build the Routh array with $K$ as a symbol
Require every first-column entry to be positive
Intersect the conditions to get the range of $K$
steps.explanation: Clear the fractions of the characteristic equation first, then the quick coefficient check often already gives one bound (e.g. $K > 0$). The Routh array gives the rest; the stable range is where all first-column conditions hold at once.

steps.prompt: Match the Routh result to the conclusion.
steps.explanation: Sign changes count right-half-plane poles; none means stable. A zero row signals symmetric roots, at a critical gain a $\pm j\omega$ pair. A coefficient with the wrong sign already fails the necessary condition.

steps.prompt: $G(s) = \frac{K}{s(s+{{a}})(s+{{b}})}$ with unity feedback and $K$ = {{K}}. Which graph is the closed-loop step response?
steps.explanation: The critical gain is $K_{crit} = {{a+b}}\cdot{{a*b}}$ = {{Km}}. Here $K$ = {{K}}, which is {{f}} × $K_{crit}$. Below $K_{crit}$ all poles are in the left half-plane and the oscillation decays; above it a complex pair has crossed into the right half-plane and the oscillation grows. Exactly at $K_{crit}$ it would oscillate with constant amplitude.
